data.title: Broken Glass
data.statement:
<<Story:>>
Sheldon bought a nice frame to incase his favourite photo. Unfortunately, on his way to the living room he accidentally tripped over something and dropped the frame, shattering the 12cm × 12cm sheet of glass inside. Now all he can see are many shards of broken glass in various orientations scattered all over the floor. The idea is ruined because Sheldon doesn't have any more money to buy another frame, that is, until he realises that he can just glue the shards back together instead. However, Sheldon is bad at jigsaw puzzles and needs some help. Can you help him?

<<Goal:>>
You are given [[n]] shards, each defined by [[m]] vertices. The shards can be thought of as 2D polygons, and vertices are points in 2D space. The coordinates of the vertices are in <<millimetres>>. The vertices of each shard form edges that are perfectly straight, going from one vertex to another. The shards will be given in various orientations and positions.

Your task is to put the shards together to form a <<12cm × 12cm>> square, and output the total length of edges that touch between two of the shards. The shards must not intersect when reassembled.

<<Additional information:>>
To help you with the implementation, the first 6 test cases gradually increase in difficulty. Out of these test cases, the first set of 3 doesn't require rotation or reflection, but the second one does. In each of both sets, the first test case has only polygons (shards) with angles that are multiples of 90°, the second one has multiples of 45°, and the third one has polygons with any angles.

To help you visualize the test cases, here's a Google document with images of them in their unsolved and solved cases:
{{https://docs.google.com/document/d/18ZscchUis7pxX-1GydIUHUax6fhGhjrCvi6JXLk11VQ/edit?usp=sharing}}

The validators might be slightly harder than the corresponding test cases, but not by much, meaning if you pass a test case, you should pass the corresponding validator as well. If that's not the case, your solution probably isn't optimized enough!

I recommend using high-precision data types to account for rounding errors.
data.constraints:
3 ≤ [[n]] ≤ 16
1 ≤ [[shard1]] < [[shard2]] ≤ [[n]]
3 ≤ [[m]] ≤ 12
-200 < [[x]], [[y]] < 200
All cases are solvable and have only one solution (ignoring all possible symmetries).
All shards are simple polygons, meaning their edges don't intersect. They also never form an angle close to 0° or 180°.
There are never two identical shards.

write 12.345
data.inputDescription:
<<Line 1:>> Integer [[n]] indicating the number of shards.
<<Line 2:>> Two space-separated integers [[shard1]] and [[shard2]] (1-indexed) specifying which shards should be used for calculating the output.
<<Next [[n]] lines:>> Integer [[m_i]] indicating the number of vertices of each shard.
<<Next line:>> Integer [[p]] being the total number of vertices.
<<Next [[p]] lines:>> [[n]] shards, each consisting of its corresponding [[m_i]] vertices.
<<- Each vertex:>> Two space-separated real coordinates [[x]] and [[y]].

The vertices of each shard are sorted in a sequential order in the clockwise direction, meaning each vertex forms an edge with the previous one, and the first one also connects to the last one.

Note: The vertices are given in the same order as the number of vertices listed for each shard. That is, if the [[n]] lines specify [[m₁]], [[m₂]], ..., [[mₙ]] vertices, then the first [[m₁]] vertex lines belong to the first shard, the next [[m₂]] to the second shard, and so on.
data.outputDescription:
The total length of edges that touch between the two shards [[shard1]] and [[shard2]], rounded to 3 decimal places. (The output should always show 3 decimal places.)
If the two shards don't touch or one touches the other by just a vertex, then the answer should be {{0.000}}.
